questions.question: When does finally run in relation to a return statement inside try?
options: Finally does not run if there is a return inside try
Finally runs before the return of the try block
Finally runs after try evaluates the return value, but before the method actually returns the result
Finally only runs when the method has no return
explanations: Finally always runs, even if there is a return in try.
Correct. When try has a return statement, finally still executes after the return value is evaluated but before the method actually returns to the caller.
Finally runs after the value to be returned is computed, not before.
Finally always runs; it does not depend on whether there is a return.

questions.question: What happens if the finally block contains a return statement?
options: The return in finally is ignored and the return in try is used
A compilation error occurs because returns are not allowed in finally
The return in finally overrides the return in try, and the method returns finally's value
Both the try return and the finally return are executed
explanations: The return in finally is not ignored; it takes priority over the one in try.
It is legal to use return in finally, but it is a bad practice because it can mask errors.
Correct. If finally has a return, it overrides the value try was going to return. This is dangerous because it can mask exceptions.
Only one return can be executed; finally overrides the one in try.

questions.question: Can try-catch blocks be nested in Java?
options: No, Java does not allow nesting try-catch
Yes, but excessive nesting is discouraged for readability
Only if a single exception type is used at each level
Only in methods that declare throws
explanations: Java does allow nesting try-catch; it is a valid feature.
Correct. You can nest try-catch, but excessive nesting makes the code harder to read and maintain.
Nesting has no restrictions on the exception types at each level.
Using throws has nothing to do with the ability to nest try-catch.

questions.question: If a method declares `catch(Exception e)`, which exceptions are NOT caught?
options: RuntimeException and all its subclasses
Only the Error and Throwable classes
All checked exceptions
None, Exception catches everything
explanations: RuntimeException is caught by catch(Exception e) because RuntimeException is a child of Exception.
Correct. Exception is the parent of all exceptions except Error and Throwable. To catch Error you need catch(Error e) or catch(Throwable e).
Exception does catch checked exceptions because they inherit from Exception.
Exception does not catch Error or Throwable directly.

questions.question: How does AutoCloseable work in try-with-resources?
options: close() is called manually at the end of the try block
Java invokes close() automatically when leaving the try-with-resources block, whether normally or due to an exception
AutoCloseable only works with streams, not with database connections
You need to use finally after try-with-resources to close the resource
explanations: With try-with-resources there is no need to call close() manually; Java does it automatically.
Correct. When a resource is declared in try-with-resources, Java invokes close() automatically when leaving the block, regardless of whether it left normally or due to an exception.
AutoCloseable works with any resource that implements the interface, not just streams.
try-with-resources already handles closing; no additional finally is needed for that.
